title: Ancilla-Depth Phase Diagrams for Quantum Reference-Frame Comparison
abstract: Comparing two noisy quantum reference frames as statistical experiments depends on the dimension of the ancillary memory available to the decision procedure. For finite-dimensional channels A and B with invertible A, we show that exact simulation of all measurements assisted by an r-dimensional ancilla is equivalent to r-positivity of the unique factor Gamma = BA^{-1}. The hierarchy can be realized by physical channel pairs: every unital, trace-preserving map that is k-positive but not (k+1)-positive embeds as the factor between the channels D_a and Gamma composed with D_a on an exact interval determined by the smallest Choi eigenvalue. For depolarizing source and target channels D_a and D_b, including negative and singular source parameters, the phase boundary is $\mathcal{D}_a \succeq_r \mathcal{D}_b \Longleftrightarrow -1/(dr-1) \leq b/a \leq 1$ for $a\neq 0$. We derive closed formulas for the restricted level-r deficiency and for the distance to every physical post-processing, $δ_{\mathrm{phys}}(\mathcal{D}_b\mid\mathcal{D}_a)=(1-1/d^2)\operatorname{dist}(b,I_a)$, where $I_a=\operatorname{conv}\{a,-a/(d^2-1)\}$. The largest physical conversion cost hidden from all tests through level k is $(d-k)/[d(d^2-1)]$. An untouched m-level spectator changes the first detecting external level from k+1 to $\lfloor k/m\rfloor+1$. A transpose--depolarizing construction shows that the separation is not confined to depolarizing factors. The results quantify the distinction between ancilla-restricted statistical simulation and implementation by a single quantum channel.
summary: This paper develops a theory to quantify when one noisy quantum channel can be statistically simulated by another, depending on the size of an auxiliary memory. It establishes criteria based on $r$-positivity and provides explicit phase diagrams for depolarizing channels. The findings are vital for understanding the distinction between theoretical simulation limits and actual physical implementability in quantum information tasks.
main_problem: The paper addresses how the comparison of two noisy quantum reference frames (channels) can be characterized by the dimension of ancillary memory available for statistical testing.
main_result: It establishes that simulation capability is equivalent to the $r$-positivity of a derived factor $\Gamma = BA^{-1}$, and quantifies physical limitations using concepts like restricted deficiency and distance to physical post-processing.
method: The analysis relies on theoretical tools including $r$-positivity criteria, Choi matrices, and deriving closed formulas for resource gaps based on the ratio of channel parameters ($\lambda=b/a$).
model_or_system: The model involves finite-dimensional quantum channels, specifically analyzing depolarizing channels ($D_\lambda$) as representative physical systems.
key_observables: Restricted level-$r$ deficiency, distance to physical post-processing ($\delta_{	ext{phys}}$), and the required ancillary dimension $r$.
important_parameters: Ancilla dimension ($r$), channel parameters ($a, b$), and the ratio $\lambda = b/a$.
main_assumptions: The results are derived for finite-dimensional models and distinguish between statistical simulation capabilities versus physical implementability via a single quantum channel.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate exact positivity bands in parameter space (e.g., $d=6$) showing how crossing boundaries activates specific ancillary witnesses, and plot the physical conversion cost $\delta_{	ext{phys}}$ vs. source parameters.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the statistical simulation problem using ancilla memory ($r$-positivity) to deriving general theorems relating this condition to factors ($\Gamma$), then applying these results specifically to depolarizing channels to map out phase diagrams, and finally quantifying physical gaps invisible at lower testing levels.
why_interesting: The work provides rigorous mathematical tools for determining the fundamental limits of quantum process comparison, which is crucial for understanding resource quantification in open quantum systems and channel characterization.
